cards.front: What does the law require in rain or reduced visibility?
cards.back: Turning on your headlights during rain or reduced visibility is required by law and increases your visibility to others.

cards.front: When is wet pavement most dangerous, and why?
cards.back: Wet pavement is most dangerous at the start of a light rain, when oil, dirt and water form a slippery film that weakens road contact on curves and lengthens stopping distance, so reduce your speed.

cards.front: At what speeds do tires wipe the road, partially hydroplane and ride on water?
cards.back: On wet pavement tires wipe the road like a windshield wiper at speeds up to thirty-five miles per hour, a standard passenger vehicle begins to hydroplane partially at about thirty-five miles per hour, and at fifty-five miles per hour the tires ride entirely on the water film, leaving no friction to brake, accelerate or corner.

cards.front: What happens in a severe rainstorm at highway speed?
cards.back: In a severe rainstorm tires lose all contact with the road at fifty-five miles per hour, and a gust of wind, a curve or a slight turn can then create an uncontrollable skid.

cards.front: How do you reduce the risk of hydroplaning?
cards.back: To reduce hydroplaning slow down in rainstorms, on slushy roads and in standing water, keep tires properly inflated and replace them when the tread wear indicators show, because deep treads let water escape and can prevent complete hydroplaning at normal highway speeds.

cards.front: Why must you never drive across a flooded roadway?
cards.back: Never drive across a flooded roadway, because as little as six inches of water can float some smaller vehicles and two feet of water will carry most vehicles away, after which the vehicle may roll and fill with water, trapping everyone inside.

cards.front: What share of flash flood deaths involve trapped motorists, and why?
cards.back: Motorists trapped in their vehicles account for nearly half of all flash flood deaths in the United States, victims often drive straight off the edge of an eroded road without knowing it is gone, and flooding is especially hard to recognize at night.

cards.front: What should you do if your vehicle stalls on a flooded road?
cards.back: If your vehicle stalls on a flooded roadway leave it immediately and seek higher ground, because it is better to be wet than dead.

cards.front: At what speeds does hydroplaning begin and become complete?
cards.back: Partial hydroplaning begins at about thirty-five miles per hour, while at fifty-five miles per hour the tires ride entirely on the water and lose all contact in a severe rainstorm.

cards.front: How much water floats small vehicles and how much carries most away?
cards.back: Six inches of water can float some smaller vehicles, whereas two feet of water will carry most vehicles away.

decks.module: Snow, ice, wind and fog techniques

cards.front: Do snow tires or chains allow normal speeds on snow, and how far can stopping take?
cards.back: Keep snow tires or chains ready in winter but remember that neither allows safe driving on snow or ice at normal speeds, so slow down and keep a safe distance, since stopping on snow or ice can take up to twelve times the normal distance and bridges and overpasses may be icy when all other pavement is clear.

cards.front: What must you do with windows, wipers and defroster in winter?
cards.back: Keep every window clear of ice and snow, keep the windshield wipers and defroster in good working order, and never start driving until all windows are clear and completely defrosted.

cards.front: How do you brake on ice with and without anti-lock brakes?
cards.back: When stopping or slowing on ice or packed snow apply the brakes gently and smoothly, a vehicle with anti-lock brakes keeps its steering while braking, but in a vehicle without them you cannot steer unless you pump the brakes by applying and releasing them several times, and you release the brakes at the first hint that the wheels are slipping.

cards.front: How do you start moving on snow or ice, and how do you test the road?
cards.back: When starting on snow or ice keep engine speed low, accelerate slowly and smoothly, let out a manual clutch slowly and shift smoothly, and once moving test the brakes at low speed to learn how slippery the road is and adjust your speed to it.

cards.front: What hazards do strong winds and crosswinds create?
cards.back: Strong winds can down power lines and trees and blow debris into your path, and crosswinds can be strong enough to force your vehicle into the oncoming lane or off the roadway.

cards.front: How do you drive in fog or dense smoke?
cards.back: Fog is extremely hazardous and smoke from factories, forest fires or burning leaves acts the same way, so in fog or dense smoke reduce speed, be ready for an emergency stop, use low-beam headlights and the wipers, and if your vision is impaired pull off the road, stop, leave the lights on and turn on the hazard lights.

cards.front: How much longer is stopping on ice, and where does ice form first?
cards.back: Stopping on snow or ice can take up to twelve times the dry-pavement distance, and bridges and overpasses freeze while other pavement stays clear.

cards.front: How does braking on ice differ with and without anti-lock brakes?
cards.back: With anti-lock brakes you brake gently and keep steering, but without them you must pump the brakes to steer and release them the moment the wheels start to slip.

cards.front: What lights and wipers do you use in fog, and when do you pull off?
cards.back: In fog or dense smoke you drive on low beams with the wipers running, and if vision is impaired you pull off and stop with both the lights and the hazard flashers on.

cards.front: What should you do when driving into sunrise or sunset glare?
cards.back: Too much natural light, such as driving east at sunrise or west at sunset, calls for the sun visor, sunglasses, reduced speed and extra alertness, and sunglasses also help on bright summer or winter days against glare from other vehicles' glass and chrome or from snow.

cards.front: When should you turn on your headlights rather than parking lights?
cards.back: At night and on overcast or rainy days turn on your headlights, not just your parking lights, as soon as it begins to get dark or whenever fog, smoke or extreme cloudiness impairs visibility, because lighting up a little early helps other drivers see you, and keep the lighting system clean and in repair.

cards.front: What does over driving your headlights mean?
cards.back: Over driving your headlights means driving too fast to stop safely within the distance your headlights clearly light.

cards.front: How do you handle oncoming headlights at night?
cards.back: Looking directly into oncoming headlights causes momentary blindness, so when meeting a vehicle at night slow down, keep to the right of your lane and look well ahead at the right edge of the road, dimming your beams within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle and within two hundred feet of a vehicle you are following.

cards.front: How do headlight dimming distances differ?
cards.back: Headlight beams are dimmed within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle but within two hundred feet of a vehicle you are following.

cards.front: How do over driving headlights and sun glare differ?
cards.back: Over driving your headlights is a too-little-light problem of speed exceeding the lit distance, while sunrise and sunset glare is a too-much-light problem answered with the visor, sunglasses and lower speed.
cards.memory_hook: Too little versus too much light

decks.module: Interstate breakdowns, fog and work zones

cards.front: What should you do if your vehicle becomes disabled on an interstate?
cards.back: Be especially alert for stopped vehicles on an interstate, and if your own vehicle becomes disabled move as far off the road as possible, turn on the four-way flashers to show that you are stopped, and get everyone out of the vehicle and well away from the road.

cards.front: Where do you place flares behind a disabled vehicle?
cards.back: Place one flare about one vehicle length behind a disabled vehicle and another about three hundred feet back, each on the shoulder near the edge of the through lane.

cards.front: What may be better to do when interstate fog is very dense?
cards.back: Fog in patches or as a haze reduces visibility, and when the fog is very dense it may be better to leave the interstate and finish the trip on slower roads.

cards.front: What should you do with your vehicle after a crash in heavy fog?
cards.back: After a crash in heavy fog get your vehicle as far off the road as possible, because leaving it on the road until the police arrive invites further crashes.

cards.front: How do you turn around on an interstate, and who may use median crossovers?
cards.back: Never make a U-turn on an interstate but go to the next exit to turn around, because the gravel or paved crossovers in highway medians are only for police and emergency vehicles.

cards.front: What must you obey in interstate construction zones, and when do you change lanes?
cards.back: Construction and maintenance zones on interstates and expressways frequently close one or more lanes and slow or stop traffic, so obey the special speed limits, traffic control signs and flaggers, and when lane-closure signs appear well in advance move to the open lane as soon as possible rather than at the last minute.

cards.front: Why must you drive cautiously in a construction zone?
cards.back: In a construction zone the route is often different, the road rougher, and large equipment and busy workers are close to your vehicle, so those workers count on you to drive cautiously and courteously and to follow the signs and flaggers that set the right speed for the conditions.

cards.front: Where do the two flares go behind a disabled vehicle?
cards.back: The first flare goes about one vehicle length behind the disabled vehicle and the second about three hundred feet back, both on the shoulder beside the through lane.

cards.front: How do you turn around on an interstate?
cards.back: Turning around on an interstate means driving to the next exit, because a U-turn is never allowed there and the median crossovers belong to police and emergency vehicles.

cards.front: What does defensive driving mean, and when do good habits begin?
cards.back: Defensive driving means being prepared through the practice of good driving habits, which are as easy to form as bad ones and should begin the moment you step into the vehicle and be used on every trip, short or long.

cards.front: Where do bad driving habits come from?
cards.back: Bad driving habits come from laziness, impatience, inattention, arrogance and aggressiveness, and a driver who shows any of them must evaluate and adjust that behavior to drive safely.

cards.front: What does a lazy driver fail to do?
cards.back: A lazy driver looks only in the rear view mirror instead of turning the head to look behind before changing lanes, pulling away from the curb or getting out on the traffic side, and failing to signal before turning, changing lanes or leaving the curb is a related bad habit that can cause a serious crash.

cards.front: What must you do at stop signs, and how does an impatient driver behave?
cards.back: Regardless of traffic you must come to a complete stop at a stop sign or red light even when turning right, and an impatient driver who speeds from stop to stop, weaves through traffic and tailgates disrupts traffic and raises the chance of a crash without realizing it.

cards.front: How does a good driver sit and pay attention?
cards.back: A good driver sits up straight with a firm grip on the wheel, knows where the vehicle is and watches developing traffic problems, because a driver who leans back, loosens the grip and lets attention wander lets the vehicle wander too, and driving with an arm out the window, chatting, gesturing or ignoring the traffic flow marks an inattentive driver.

cards.front: How does an arrogant or aggressive driver differ from an impatient one?
cards.back: While the impatient driver is simply in a hurry, the arrogant or aggressive driver is purposely in a hurry, treats the vehicle as an extension of the ego, shows little respect for traffic laws or the rights of others, and should neither be imitated nor competed with.

cards.front: Why is concentration so important while driving?
cards.back: Concentration is one of the most important elements of safe driving, so the driver's seat is no place for daydreaming, mental napping, window shopping, scenic viewing or distracting conversation, because driving an automobile is a full-time job.

cards.front: Does a right turn excuse a full stop at a stop sign?
cards.back: Pressure from vehicles behind and an empty cross street tempt the impatient driver merely to slow for a stop sign, yet a complete stop is required at every stop sign or red light even for a right turn.

cards.front: How does an impatient driver differ from an aggressive one?
cards.back: The impatient driver is simply in a hurry, whereas the arrogant or aggressive driver is purposely in a hurry and treats the vehicle as an extension of the ego.

cards.front: Which road conditions should a driver consider?
cards.back: Road conditions to consider are mainly matters of construction such as curves, hills, pavement width, multiple lanes, road surfaces, poorly marked or unmarked roads, shoulders and drop-offs.

cards.front: How often must a vehicle be inspected, and what does the sticker show?
cards.back: You cannot safely drive ten feet or ten miles in an unsafe vehicle, so West Virginia requires every vehicle to be inspected every two years at a station displaying the official state inspection sign, and the windshield sticker showing the month and year of the next inspection must never be removed.

cards.front: How often is inspection due, and may the sticker be removed?
cards.back: A state inspection is due every two years and its windshield sticker shows the month and year of the next one, and removing that sticker is against the law.
